title: MONITORING AND MANAGING LINUX PROCESSES
display: Ch 8 — MONITORING AND MANAGING LINUX PROCESSES

content.text: Book reference: Chapter 8, pages 239–286. Guided Exercises: Controlling Jobs, Killing Processes, Monitoring Process Activity. Lab: Monitoring and Managing Linux Processes.
RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — This whole chapter

Listing, backgrounding, and killing processes by signal is routine, hands-on RHCSA material — and process troubleshooting ("why is this server slow") is a real-world skill the exam is deliberately designed to test.

Every running program is a process: an address space, ownership/security credentials, one or more threads of execution, and a state. A parent process forks (duplicates itself) to create a child, which then usually execs its own program code. Every process on the system descends from PID 1 — systemd on RHEL 8.

When a child exits, it becomes a zombie — an entry in the process table with nothing left but its PID — until its parent "reaps" it (acknowledges the exit) and the entry is fully released. A pile-up of zombie processes almost always means a buggy parent that isn't reaping its children, not a problem with the zombies themselves.
Process states
| Flag | Name | Meaning |
| `R` | Running | Executing on a CPU, or ready and waiting for one |
| `S` | Sleeping (interruptible) | Waiting on some condition (I/O, a signal); returns to Running once satisfied |
| `D` | Sleeping (uninterruptible) | Also waiting, but won't respond to signals — reserved for waits where interrupting mid-operation could leave a device in a bad state |
| `T` | Stopped | Suspended, usually by a signal (e.g. Ctrl+Z); resumes on another signal |
| `Z` | Zombie | Exited; every resource released except the process-table entry itself, pending the parent's cleanup |
NOTE — A single CPU never runs several R-state processes at once
Seeing several processes in state R at once on a single-CPU system doesn't mean they're all executing simultaneously — only one can run at any instant; the rest are ready and queued.
Listing processes with ps
WARNING — Three option styles, and they don't mix the way you'd expect

ps supports UNIX options (-ef, single dash), BSD options (aux, no dash), and GNU long options (--sort, double dash). ps -aux and ps aux are NOT the same command — mixing a dash onto a BSD-style option string changes its meaning. Pick one style and stick with it: aux or -ef are both fine, common choices.
| Command | Shows |
| `ps` | Just your own processes attached to the current terminal |
| `ps aux` | Every process on the system, including ones with no controlling terminal |
| `ps -ef` | Same coverage as aux, UNIX-style column layout |
| `ps lax` | Long format — more technical detail, and faster since it skips username lookups |

Default sort order is by PID, which looks chronological but isn't guaranteed — PIDs get reused as old processes exit, so don't rely on ps order to reconstruct a timeline. Use -O or --sort explicitly if order actually matters.

sections.title: 8.2 Job control — running several things from one shell

content.text: A job is whatever you entered at one prompt — a single command or a whole pipeline — tracked as one unit by that shell session. Only one job at a time can be in the foreground of a terminal (reading keyboard input); everything else is in the background.
| Action | How |
| Start already in the background | `append & to the command` |
| Suspend the foreground job | `Ctrl+Z (sends SIGTSTP — stops it, doesn't kill it)` |
| List this session's jobs | `jobs` |
| Resume a stopped job in the background | `bg %jobnumber (or bg for the default job)` |
| Bring a background job to the foreground | `fg %jobnumber` |
The + next to a job number in jobs marks the default job — the one bg/fg act on if you don't specify a number.
RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — Exiting a terminal with jobs still suspended
Bash warns you once if you try to exit with stopped jobs present. Exiting again immediately kills them — worth knowing before you accidentally lose a suspended process you meant to keep.
Processes with no controlling terminal (system daemons, started by systemd rather than a shell) show a ? in ps's TTY column — they're not part of any job and can never be brought to a foreground.

sections.title: 8.3 Signals — the real language of process control

content.text: A signal is a software interrupt delivered to a process — from the kernel, another process, or a keyboard shortcut. Programs can accept a signal's default behavior, or handle/ignore/replace it themselves (except for the two that can never be intercepted).
RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — The signals you must know cold
This is the single highest-value table in this chapter — every one of these appears in real troubleshooting and on the exam.
| Number | Name | Effect |
| 1 | `SIGHUP` | Hangup — historically "controlling terminal closed"; commonly repurposed to mean "reload your config" without restarting |
| 2 | `SIGINT` | Ctrl+C — interrupt; can be blocked or handled |
| 3 | `SIGQUIT` | Ctrl+\ — like SIGINT but also dumps a core file |
| 9 | `SIGKILL` | Unconditional, unblockable, unhandleable termination — always fatal, no cleanup runs |
| 15 | `SIGTERM` | The polite request to terminate — the default for kill and the one to try FIRST; can be caught, letting a program clean up before exiting |
| 18 | `SIGCONT` | Resume a stopped process; can't be blocked |
| 19 | `SIGSTOP` | Unconditional suspend; can't be blocked or handled |
| 20 | `SIGTSTP` | Ctrl+Z — the polite, catchable version of SIGSTOP |
WARNING — Don't reach for SIGKILL first

SIGKILL is commonly overused. Because the target process gets no chance to run its own cleanup (closing files, releasing locks, flushing writes), it should be a last resort. The recommended order is SIGTERM first, then SIGINT, and only escalate to SIGKILL (kill -9 or kill -SIGKILL) if the process genuinely won't respond to either.
Commands for sending signals
| Command | Targets by | Example |
| `kill` | PID number | `kill -15 5194 (or kill -TERM 5194 — plain kill with no signal already sends TERM)` |
| `killall` | Command name, all matches | `killall control` |
| `pkill` | Pattern match: command, user (-u), group (-g), parent PID (-P), terminal (-t) | `pkill -u bob / pkill -P 8391` |
| `pgrep` | Same matching options as pkill, but LISTS PIDs instead of signaling them | `pgrep -l -u bob` |
RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — Standard workflow: pgrep to find, then pkill to act

A reliable pattern for the exam: run pgrep -l -u username first to see exactly what you're about to signal, THEN pkill with the same selection criteria once you've confirmed the target list is correct — rather than guessing and firing blind.
kill -l lists every signal name and number available on the system, if you ever need to look one up.
Logging a user out administratively
w shows who's logged in, their TTY, where they connected from, and their load average, JCPU/PCPU usage — everything you need to identify a session before acting on it.
w
pgrep -l -u bob # see exactly what belongs to bob before touching anything
pkill -SIGKILL -u bob # kill everything bob owns, including his login shell
💡 Why this matters — Why SIGKILL specifically for a whole login session

A session leader (the login shell itself) is deliberately built to survive and ignore ordinary termination signals, since accidental keyboard signals shouldn't kill your whole session. To force out an entire session including that shell, SIGKILL is genuinely required — a plain SIGTERM will clear out the user's other processes but leave the login shell standing.

To target only processes on one specific terminal (leaving that user's login shell alive on other terminals untouched): pkill -t tty3. To target only children of a specific process (leaving the parent shell alive): find the parent with pstree -p username, then pkill -P <parent-pid>.

Load average is the kernel's own rough estimate of demand: every 5 seconds it counts processes in state R (ready to run) or D (waiting on I/O) and reports an exponential moving average over the last 1, 5, and 15 minutes. Unlike some other UNIX systems, Linux deliberately counts I/O-bound waiting alongside CPU-bound waiting — a disk or network bottleneck shows up in load average just as much as CPU contention does, which is exactly why a high load average with low CPU usage is a real, meaningful signal (check disk/network activity, not just the CPU).
uptime
# 15:29:03 up 14 min, 2 users, load average: 2.92, 4.48, 5.20

The three numbers are 1-, 5-, and 15-minute averages, in that order — comparing them tells you whether load is currently rising or falling. To judge whether a raw number is actually a problem, divide by the CPU count from lscpu: a per-CPU value below 1 means the system is comfortably keeping up; above 1 means requests are queuing and something is waiting.
RHCSA EXAM CRITICAL — Reading load average correctly is a real diagnostic skill, not just a number to quote

A load average of 2.92 on a 4-CPU box (0.73 per CPU) is comfortable. The same 2.92 on a 2-CPU box (1.46 per CPU) means the system is oversaturated. Never judge a load average number without also checking lscpu.
top — the dynamic view
Where ps is a single snapshot, top refreshes continuously and lets you sort/filter/act interactively.
| Key | Effect |
| `Shift+M` | Sort by memory usage, descending |
| `Shift+P` | Sort by CPU usage, descending |
| `u` | Filter to one user |
| `k` | Kill a process — prompts for PID, then signal |
| `r` | Renice a process — prompts for PID, then nice value |
| `1` | Toggle per-core vs. summary CPU view in the header |
| `q` | Quit |
top's columns map directly onto ps's, with different names: VIRT = ps's VSZ (virtual memory), RES = ps's RSS (physical memory actually resident).

sections.title: Hands-on: practice these on your own lab

content.text: 1. ssh student@servera; sleep 300 & — note the job number and PID printed.
2. jobs — confirm it's listed as Running; Ctrl+Z on a separate foreground sleep 300 to see Stopped state, then bg %1 to resume it in the background.
3. ps aux | grep sleep to find the PID directly, then kill -15 <PID> — confirm with jobs that it terminated.

4. Start three background sleeps, then practice pgrep -l -u student to see all three, followed by pkill -u student (careful — logged-in-session-aware; test this on a disposable VM) to clear them at once.
5. uptime, then lscpu — divide the 1-minute load average by the CPU count and decide whether the system is currently under real pressure.
6. top, press Shift+M to sort by memory, then q to quit.
1. Q1 — A process refuses to respond to kill -15. What should you try next, and only as a last resort after that?
2. Q2 — You need to end an entire user's login session, including their shell itself, not just their background jobs. Which signal is required, and why won't a gentler one work here?
3. Q3 — A server's load average is 6.0 on an 8-CPU box, mostly from processes in state D, not R. What does that tell you about where to look for the bottleneck?
NOTE — Answers
Q1 — Try SIGINT next, and only escalate to SIGKILL (kill -9) if that also fails — SIGKILL skips the process's own cleanup entirely, so it's a last resort, not a first move.

Q2 — SIGKILL. The session leader (login shell) is specifically designed to survive and ignore ordinary signals like SIGTERM, precisely so accidental keyboard interrupts don't kill your whole session — only the unblockable SIGKILL can force it out.

Q3 — Mostly-D-state load points at I/O wait (disk or network), not CPU contention — 6.0/8 = 0.75 per CPU would look totally fine if it were CPU-bound, so the actual bottleneck to investigate is storage or network throughput, not processor capacity.
- A process is a running program instance with a state (R/S/D/T/Z); ps lists them, with aux or -ef as the common full-listing styles — don't mix option conventions.
- Job control (&, Ctrl+Z, jobs, bg, fg) manages multiple commands from one shell session; only one job can be foreground at a time.
- Signals control processes: SIGTERM (15) is the polite default, SIGKILL (9) is the unblockable last resort — try TERM, then INT, before ever reaching for KILL.
- kill targets a PID; killall and pkill target by name/user/parent/terminal; pgrep lists matches without acting, and is the safe way to check a target list before pkill acts on it.
- Load average (1/5/15-minute, from uptime, w, or top) counts both CPU-ready (R) and I/O-waiting (D) processes — divide by CPU count from lscpu before judging whether a number is actually a problem.
